extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, pop-culture listicles, and examples of comic insults
extracted.subtask_description: A ranked listicle collecting and showcasing the 'harshest' insults comedians have directed at other comedians, with brief context for each example. Primarily for entertainment and as examples of comedian-on-comedian ribbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harshness / severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of cruelty or severity of the jab — the article is explicitly titled 'The 30 Harshest Comedian-on-Comedian Insults in History' and ranks examples by how harsh they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples range from snide one-liners to profanity-laced attacks (e.g., 'Fuckin’ Leary. Fuckin’ talentless cunt.'), indicating that raw viciousness or blunt cruelty is the primary axis for selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed at fellow comedians
rubrics_metrics.description: Insult must be 'comedian-on-comedian' — aimed at another performer in the same profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every entry targets another comic (e.g., Patton Oswalt on David Cross; Joan Rivers on Chelsea Handler); the list focuses on intra-industry rivalries, feuds, and ribbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit / sharpness of phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleverness, punch, and turn-of-phrase — the intro highlights 'sharp wits' as a source of excellent insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many selections rely on concise, witty comparisons or wordplay (e.g., 'You can talk about love all you want. To me, you’re nothing but a fucking dollar sign.'), so incisive phrasing is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context / public forum of delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the insult was delivered — roasts, TV appearances, podcasts, Twitter, interviews — the medium/context contributes to impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intro calls out 'Comedy Central roasts to Jay ‘n’ Conan to Twitter spats' as typical settings; context (live roast vs. private remark vs. broadcast) affects visibility and perceived harshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchiness / brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, memorable one-liners and concise put-downs that land quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list favors succinct quips that are easily repeatable (e.g., 'He couldn’t ad-lib a fart after a baked-bean dinner.'), suggesting economy of words is a valued trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal / professional humiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacks that target the target's talent, career, reputation, or personal attributes rather than abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many insults accuse targets of being untalented, derivative, or professionally washed-up (e.g., 'You made us all laugh so much… and then inexplicably stopped in about 1978.'), showing that hits at career/status amplify harshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of profanity and explicit language
rubrics_metrics.description: Crude or profane language is commonly used to increase forcefulness and shock value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several top entries include strong profanity (e.g., 'talentless cunt', 'motherfucker'), indicating that explicitness is part of what the article counts as 'harsh.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical / cultural comparisons and similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons to cultural figures, objects, or scenarios to emphasize ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insults often use vivid comparisons (e.g., 'You look like Krusty the Clown dressed as Joe Paterno.'; 'triangle-headed Eddie Murphy look-alike motherfucker'), showing that evocative similes increase memorability and sting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation of persona or appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mocking a comedian's persona, voice, mannerisms, or physical appearance as the core of the insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several entries lampoon a comic's public persona or look (e.g., references to being 'a bitter Jewish comedian', 'triangle-headed'), implying that targeting identity/branding is an effective tactic.
